title: None like our God
hookLine: a simple song with a repeating tune

cards: Some songs are built to be learned in one hearing. A lullaby. A chant at a ball game.
Ein Keloheinu is one of those. Someone who can't read a word of Hebrew can join in by the second verse.
The same handful of words come around again and again, with only the first word changing, and the familiar Ashkenazi tune rolls along like a march.
But the simple song hides a puzzle in its order, and a word hidden in its first letters.

teach.b: Ein keloheinu means there is none like our God. The song goes: none like our God, none like our Lord, none like our King, none like our Savior. The next verse swaps the first word: who is like our God?
Then: let us give thanks to our God. Then: blessed is our God. And last: you are our God.
Five verses, four names each time. Here's the puzzle.

teach.h: FIRST THE ANSWER, THEN THE QUESTION.
teach.b: Why say there is none like our God first, and only then ask who is like our God? Shouldn't the question come before the answer?

One explanation from the commentators: the song states it first, so that when it asks, the question is wonder, not doubt. The singer already holds the answer, and asks for the joy of asking. Now the secret.
Take the first letters of the first three verses in Hebrew: ein, mi, nodeh. Aleph, mem, nun.
Together they spell amen, the word people say to agree with a blessing. There's one more explanation people give. On weekdays the main prayer has nineteen blessings, but on Shabbat only seven.
Some say this song, with its many names of God, helps make up the hundred blessings the Talmud asks for each day.
Customs differ: Ashkenazim usually sing it near the end of Shabbat and festival mornings, and many Sephardim say it every day. Either way, it's twenty names of God, carried on one easy tune.

how: Ein Keloheinu is sung near the end of the Shabbat and festival morning service in most Ashkenazi synagogues, and said daily in many Sephardi communities; it is usually followed by a Talmud passage about the Temple incense.

games.q: inside Ein Keloheinu — tap the pairs.

s: the song asks who is like our God before it answers

the first letters of the first three verses spell amen
aleph, mem, nun: ein, mi, nodeh.
many Sephardim say it every day.

games.q: you're writing a song of praise. do you ask who is like our God first, or declare none like our God first?
games.why: the song declares first. commentators say that way the question is wonder, not doubt.

practice: Choose one short line, ein keloheinu, or the English, none like our God, or any line that means something to you, and say or sing it slowly, again and again, adding nothing.
Let the repetition do the work, and notice whether the words grow lighter, or heavier, or simply quieter.
